drafts.accepts: Any named method for designing or running software tests that is described in the testing literature or a standards document.
Any named program whose main purpose is editing plain text files, whether terminal, GUI, or historical, such as Notepad or ed.
Any named software that records and manages revisions of a file tree, centralized or distributed, current or historical, such as RCS or Perforce.
Any named plugin for Vim or Neovim published on GitHub or a plugin manager index, which a judge can look up by name.
Any named software framework for building web applications or HTTP services, in any language, that is documented or published.
Any named software that accepts and answers HTTP requests, current or historical.
Any attribute type name in the IANA BGP Path Attributes registry.
Any named policy that decides which cached item to evict, whether in OS page caches, hardware caches or software caches.
Any named algorithm or policy that selects which runnable task gets the CPU next, from textbooks, research papers or OS source code.
Any option name in the IANA BOOTP and DHCP parameters registry or the DHCP option lists in RFC 2132 and its successors.
Any resource record type with a registered TYPE number in the IANA DNS parameters registry.
Any authentication method registered with IANA for the Extensible Authentication Protocol or defined in an RFC for EAP.
Any section name defined in the ELF specification, the System V gABI, or a toolchain or ABI extension for ELF object files.
Any named erasure or RAID-style coding scheme from coding theory or storage literature that adds redundancy to recover lost blocks.
Any published IEEE 802 standard or amendment, identified by its 802.x number.

drafts.prompt: Name a Linux kernel boot parameter
drafts.accepts: Any option documented in the kernel's admin-guide kernel-parameters list that can be passed on the kernel command line.
Any CAP_ name defined in capabilities(7) for the current Linux kernel.
Any path under /dev that the Linux kernel or a driver creates as a character or block device node, such as the names documented in the kernel or devices.txt.
Any E-prefixed error constant defined in the Linux errno-base or errno headers.
Any ioctl request constant defined in Linux uapi headers, such as those under linux/fs.h, linux/fd.h or asm-generic/ioctls.h.
